The difference between typicality and family resemblance is that (2 pts.)
a) Typical instances are more likely to be classified as members of the category,
whereas instances of a family resemblance category are likely to be classified as
members of other categories.
b) Typicality reflects the goodness of category membership, whereas family
resemblance reflects the likelihood of category membership.
c) Typicality tells you which instances are more typical and family resemblance tells
you which members have more resemblance to the family.
d) Typicality tells you which instances are more typical and family resemblance tells
you which members are more likely to resemble other categories

Please write in English language.
rounds.assistant:
The difference between typicality and family resemblance is that:

b) Typicality reflects the goodness of category membership, whereas family resemblance reflects the likelihood of category membership.

Typicality refers to how well an object or concept fits into a specific category, with more typical instances being more representative of the category. It reflects the degree to which an object or concept possesses the defining features of the category. Family resemblance, on the other hand, refers to the similarity between members of a category based on a range of shared features, rather than a set of defining features. It reflects the degree to which members of a category share overlapping features and characteristics.

Therefore, while typicality reflects how good a fit an object is for a specific category, family resemblance reflects how likely it is that an object belongs to a category based on its shared features and characteristics with other members of that category.

Gain Frame:
Option A: 100% chance 200 lives saved = 200 lives saved
Option B: 1/3 probability that 600 people will be saved + 2/3 probability that no one is saved = (1/3 \* 600) + (2/3 \* 0) = 200 lives saved
Total expected utility for gain frame = 400 lives saved

Loss Frame:
Option C: 100% chance 400 will die = -400 lives saved
Option D: 1/3 probability that nobody will die + 2/3 probability that 600 people will die = (1/3 \* 0) + (2/3 \* -600) = -400 lives saved
Total expected utility for loss frame = -800 lives saved

In the gain frame, participants tend to choose either option A or B, both of which offer positive expected utility in terms of lives saved. In the loss frame, participants tend to choose option C, which minimizes the number of lives lost, despite having a lower expected utility than option A or B. Option D in the loss frame is often seen as too risky and is therefore less frequently chosen.
